title: Pure-C# decoupling + headless fuzz tests with coding agents to solve 2D light popping across 1,000+ falling-sand fluid lights in Godot 4
author: will-QA-for-food
selftext:
Working on Nine Lives Below, a 1-4 player co-op wizard cat game inspired by Noita mechanics. 

**What was the problem?**

Godot has a 2D rendering limit where a single canvas item can only be lit by at most 16 PointLight sources at once.

**What was the solution?**

Because our destructible terrain renders as 64x64 chunk Sprite2Ds, as soon as many light sources (i.e. lava, acid, projectiles) piled up in the same space the chunks would start to flicker as the viewport moved. This was resolved by using a few different optimization methods.

Instead of spawning lights per glowing pixel we scan the 64x64 cells to group emissive pixels into weighted center of mass emitters with stable 64-bit IDs. Since Godot breaks at 16 lights per chunk, we normally cap each chunk at **13** lights. That leaves 2 "spare" slots (14 and 15) reserved just for older lights to fade out smoothly over a split second when a brighter light moves in so lights never snap on or off abruptly.

**What worked on the AI workflow side?**

There were a couple guardrails that made coding agents effective on a system like this:

* Pure C# Core and 100% simulated world, agents were able to write/run headless tests without needing to boot up the engine every loop.
* In game diagnostic overlays and keyframe dumps, having the agents add overlays to our testing  simulations allowed us to visually verify the runs and compare deterministic PNG keyframes against each other.

Happy to answer more questions about the overall design of the test harness and setup.
